paragraphs: The paper studies a sampling problem in which a learner must identify every option whose average outcome exceeds a specified threshold. Each option, called an arm, produces uncertain observations. The learner has a fixed sampling budget and only needs to classify the arms up to a requested precision. The objective is therefore to learn which arms qualify, rather than to maximize rewards while collecting observations.

The authors introduce a parameter-free algorithm based on a new heuristic for choosing what to sample. This addresses the central allocation question: how should limited observations be distributed across arms to identify the qualifying set? The algorithm is designed specifically for the thresholding objective and its fixed time horizon.

The main finding is a proof of optimality through matching upper and lower bounds. These bounds establish both what the proposed method can achieve and the corresponding difficulty of the problem. The authors qualify their historical claim: to their knowledge, this is the first nontrivial fixed-budget pure-exploration setting with a provably optimal strategy.
icml-2016-an-optimal-algorithm-for-the-t.tldr: A parameter-free sampling algorithm provably optimally identifies which bandit arms exceed a threshold within a fixed budget and specified precision.

paragraphs: Sparse matrix factorization breaks a data matrix into components that can provide an interpretable description of its structure. It can also support filling in missing entries and removing noise. The paper addresses a computational obstacle that arises when a matrix is enormous in both dimensions, so reducing the cost associated with only one dimension leaves a substantial bottleneck.

The authors propose a factorization method intended to scale to terabyte-sized datasets. Their starting observation is that existing online and randomized approaches reduce complexity along one matrix dimension without doing so along both. The contribution is therefore about making factorization practical for a broader size regime, including datasets that previous algorithms could not process within a reasonable time.

The method is evaluated on massive functional magnetic resonance imaging data and on recommendation problems involving matrix completion. The authors report significant speed improvements over state-of-the-art coordinate descent methods. These findings support the method’s computational value for the tested applications, where both dimensions of the data make conventional factorization expensive.
icml-2016-dictionary-learning-for-massiv.tldr: A sparse matrix factorization method handles matrices that are massive in both dimensions, with substantial reported speedups on imaging and recommendation tasks.

paragraphs: This paper treats binary and multiclass classification through the geometry of predicted class probabilities. A classifier assigns probabilities to labels as its input changes. The authors view that probability estimator as defining a geometric surface, or submanifold, and propose controlling its complexity by penalizing the surface’s volume.

The motivating intuition is that overfitting creates rapid local fluctuations in predicted probabilities. Those fluctuations enlarge the associated surface, so a volume penalty discourages this kind of behavior. The regularizer thus connects the shape of the probability function to a measure of model complexity. It supplies a common geometric perspective for classification with either two classes or several.

The approach applies to classification functions that meet two explicit requirements: class probabilities must be available, and their first and second derivatives must be calculable. The authors combine the regularizer with standard classification losses. In experiments, their radial-basis-function implementation compares favorably with widely used regularization methods on both binary and multiclass tasks, providing empirical support for the geometric approach.
icml-2016-differential-geometric-regular.tldr: Penalizing the geometric volume of a classifier’s probability surface provides a regularizer that performs favorably in binary and multiclass experiments.

paragraphs: The paper develops scalable versions of extended and unscented Gaussian process methods that can predict multiple outputs. The original methods accommodate general likelihood models by approximating how those models behave within variational inference. They use either a Taylor-series linearization or the Unscented Transform, allowing the inference procedure to work with likelihoods beyond a narrowly restricted form.

The authors build their generalization around random-feature approximations to Gaussian process covariance functions. These approximations provide the computational foundation for reducing the cost of the original methods while extending them to multiple outputs. The approach brings together flexible likelihood handling, approximate Gaussian process computation, and the ability to address tasks with several related prediction targets.

On small single-task problems, the proposed methods can achieve performance similar to that of the original algorithms at lower computational cost. The authors also evaluate them at larger scale on MNIST and on seismic inversion, which is inherently a multitask problem. Together, these evaluations address both the cost of the approximation and its use beyond small, single-output settings.
icml-2016-extended-and-unscented-kitchen.tldr: Random-feature approximations make extended and unscented Gaussian process methods more scalable and support multiple outputs.

paragraphs: Mechanistic models built from coupled differential equations describe how interacting quantities change over time. Inferring their parameters requires reconciling observed data with the dynamics specified by those equations. This paper proposes a method for that task that combines kernel ridge regression with gradient matching, connecting fitted trajectories to the rates of change required by the model.

Its objective has two complementary roles: it rewards a good fit to observations and penalizes disagreement with the differential equations. This makes consistency with the proposed mechanism part of the fitting process. The method therefore considers both how well a trajectory follows the data and how well its changes agree with the equations.

For fast optimization, the authors exploit partial convexity within the objective and construct an iterative procedure resembling the EM algorithm. Partial convexity supplies useful structure without implying that the entire inference problem is convex. Evaluations on several benchmark datasets suggest favorable comparisons with state-of-the-art alternatives, supporting the method as a promising approach to efficient parameter inference.
icml-2016-fast-parameter-inference-in-no.tldr: An iterative gradient-matching method fits nonlinear dynamical models by balancing agreement with observations against consistency with differential equations.

paragraphs: ForecastICU is a decision-support system that follows hospitalized patients’ physiological measurements and raises alarms about future intensive care admission. During offline training, it constructs a Bayesian belief system linking patterns over time in those measurements to clinical status. Its prediction process therefore uses evolving physiological trajectories.

For a new patient, the system updates its belief about clinical status as measurements arrive. An alarm occurs when that belief reaches a predefined confidence threshold. This connects the timing of an alert to the accumulation of evidence and makes ongoing belief updates central to the monitoring procedure.

Using data from UCLA Ronald Reagan Medical Center, the authors report predictions nine hours before physicians’ admission decisions at 40% sensitivity and 50% precision. Against the best compared machine learning algorithm, they report predictions three hours earlier, a 7.8% sensitivity gain, and a 5.1% precision gain. They also report a 22.3% AUC gain over the Rothman index. These results describe predictive performance in the evaluated dataset; the nine-hour finding is tied to its stated sensitivity and precision.
icml-2016-forecasticu-a-prognostic-decis.tldr: ForecastICU updates Bayesian beliefs from patient measurements and predicted ICU admission nine hours before physicians’ decisions at 40% sensitivity and 50% precision.

paragraphs: Many machine learning computations require a scalar expression of the form uᵀA⁻¹u, where A is a positive definite matrix and u is a supplied vector. Although the output is just one number, obtaining it can be computationally demanding for large matrices. This paper develops a framework based on Gauss-type quadrature to accelerate algorithms that need these expressions.

The framework scales to large, sparse matrices and supports retrospective computation of lower and upper bounds on the desired value. The authors prove that the bounds become tighter with successive iterations and converge at a geometric rate. This supplies progressively more precise information about the quantity, together with a theoretical description of how quickly that precision improves.

The authors use the framework to accelerate tasks involving determinantal point processes and submodular optimization, reporting very large speedups in several instances. They also identify the bound-tightening and convergence results as, to their knowledge, new properties established for Gauss-type quadrature. The contribution connects those theoretical guarantees to practical savings inside larger machine learning algorithms.
icml-2016-gaussian-quadrature-for-matrix.tldr: Gauss-type quadrature yields progressively tighter bounds on matrix inverse expressions and accelerates several machine learning computations.

paragraphs: Hierarchical Poisson factorization models user and item behavior in very sparse matrices, making it useful for recommendation. Its Gamma-Poisson structure supports scalable computation, but it tightly links two modeling questions: whether a rating is absent and what value a rating takes. That coupling restricts how flexibly the model can describe observed responses.

The proposed hierarchical compound Poisson factorization separates the sparsity model from the response model while retaining the favorable hierarchical structure and scalability. This separation allows the response distribution to be chosen to suit the data. The model can represent binary outcomes, non-negative discrete values, non-negative continuous values, and continuous responses with an excess of zeros.

The authors compare the new model with hierarchical Poisson factorization on nine discrete and three continuous datasets. They conclude that the compound model better captures the relationship between sparsity and response. The practical significance is a more adaptable treatment of values in extremely sparse data, while preserving the computational structure that makes the original model useful.
icml-2016-hierarchical-compound-poisson-.tldr: Hierarchical compound Poisson factorization separates sparsity from response modeling, supporting more varied data distributions while retaining scalability.

paragraphs: The paper investigates how to learn a Granger causality graph for Hawkes processes, a particular class of models for events occurring over time. It connects the graph to the process’s impact functions, which describe triggering relationships. This link makes it possible to estimate which process dimensions are connected while also learning the temporal patterns of their influence.

The authors express each impact function as a combination of basis functions. They recover graph structure by encouraging groups of the corresponding coefficients to be sparse. Their learning algorithm combines maximum likelihood estimation with a sparse-group-lasso regularizer, joining data fit with structured selection of relationships. When clustering information is available, it can also incorporate pairwise similarity between process dimensions.

The paper analyzes the learning method and discusses how to choose the basis functions. Experiments using synthetic and real-world data show that it can recover both the Granger causality graph and triggering patterns. Its scope is specifically Hawkes processes, providing a targeted approach to a problem that is difficult for general point processes.
icml-2016-learning-granger-causality-for.tldr: Structured sparsity in Hawkes process impact functions enables joint learning of Granger causality graphs and temporal triggering patterns.

paragraphs: Matrix eigen-decomposition is a core operation in scientific computing and machine learning, but large datasets create demands that existing methods do not adequately address. This paper approaches the inherently nonconvex problem through optimization on Riemannian manifolds. It introduces DSRG-EIGS, an eigensolver designed to reduce the computational burden of each optimization iteration.

The method combines two sources of randomness. It generalizes stochastic Euclidean gradient ascent and stochastic Euclidean coordinate ascent to the Riemannian setting. This combination is the basis of its description as doubly stochastic. According to the authors, it substantially reduces per-iteration complexity and avoids matrix inversion entirely, two properties that make the method suitable for large-scale applications.

The authors theoretically analyze convergence and evaluate the solver on real-world datasets. They report encouraging advantages over deterministic counterparts. The significance is both algorithmic and empirical: the method changes how work is allocated within each iteration, and the experiments support the usefulness of that change. The reported comparisons establish benefits in the evaluated settings rather than a universal advantage for every matrix.
icml-2016-matrix-eigen-decomposition-via.tldr: A doubly stochastic Riemannian eigensolver lowers per-iteration cost, avoids matrix inversion, and shows advantages over deterministic methods.

paragraphs: The paper addresses learning from very few examples, a setting that challenges neural networks relying on extensive gradient-based training. Incorporating new information through repeated parameter learning can be inefficient and can interfere with information already learned. Memory-augmented architectures offer a way to encode and retrieve fresh information quickly, creating a possible route around those difficulties.

The authors demonstrate a memory-augmented neural network that rapidly absorbs new data and uses it to make accurate predictions after only a few samples. The central idea is to give the network access to stored information that can support predictions as new examples arrive. This focuses the learning problem on effective use of memory as well as the network’s learned parameters.

The paper also introduces a method for accessing external memory based on its content. Earlier approaches additionally used mechanisms that focused on memory locations. The demonstrated few-sample predictions support the value of augmented memory for rapid learning, while the content-focused access method provides a specific architectural contribution to that capability.
icml-2016-meta-learning-with-memory-augm.tldr: A memory-augmented neural network rapidly incorporates new examples and makes accurate few-sample predictions using content-focused external memory access.

paragraphs: This paper introduces a variational inference framework for text models with hidden, or latent, variables. Such models require approximations to distributions that are difficult to compute directly. The authors use an inference network that takes discrete text as input and produces the variational distribution, making the approximation itself a learned component of the model.

The framework supports both generative and conditional text modeling. For document generation, the authors combine a continuous stochastic representation of a document with a bag-of-words generative model. This application learns a probabilistic document representation and uses it within a model of word content. It achieves the lowest reported perplexities on two standard test corpora.

The second application is supervised answer selection. Here, a stochastic representation layer sits within an attention mechanism to capture the semantic relationship between a question and an answer. The model exceeds previously published benchmark results on two question-answering datasets. These two applications demonstrate the framework’s usefulness across distinct text tasks, with reported improvements in both document modeling and answer selection.
icml-2016-neural-variational-inference-f.tldr: Text-conditioned inference networks support probabilistic document modeling and answer selection, with leading reported results on the evaluated benchmarks.

paragraphs: The paper considers linear regression when the number of potential predictors exceeds the number of observations. Ordinary least squares is not directly applicable in the usual way in this regime. The authors advocate a generalized version inspired by ridge regression, aiming to retain the intuitive and computational appeal of least-squares fitting for high-dimensional problems.

They propose two algorithms, each consisting of three steps and combining least-squares fitting with hard thresholding. Thresholding supplies a direct selection mechanism by retaining or removing fitted components according to a cutoff. Together, these operations provide a simple route from fitting a large model to selecting its relevant variables. The authors emphasize that the procedures are understandable and can be implemented efficiently.

The methods also have theoretical appeal for consistent model selection. Simulations and data analyses compare them with penalization-based approaches and illustrate their potential. The contribution is a pair of straightforward high-dimensional regression procedures supported by theory and numerical evidence, with the empirical findings presented as promising rather than as a universal superiority claim.
icml-2016-no-penalty-no-tears-least-squa.tldr: Two simple algorithms combine generalized least squares with hard thresholding for high-dimensional regression and model selection.

paragraphs: Graduated optimization, also called continuation, is a popular approach to nonconvex optimization whose convergence behavior has received limited theoretical explanation. This paper develops a new first-order algorithm based on that approach and identifies a family of nonconvex functions for which global convergence can be proved. The guarantee is explicitly tied to this characterized family.

For those problems, the authors show that the method reaches an ε-approximate solution within O(1/ε²) gradient-based steps. This gives a quantitative relationship between the requested accuracy and the number of optimization steps. They also extend the algorithm and analysis to stochastic optimization with noisy gradient feedback, obtaining the same stated convergence rate.

The paper additionally considers zero-order optimization, where the method must work without gradient feedback, and provides a variant with rate O(d²/ε⁴). The contribution is therefore a set of guarantees across different information settings. It establishes circumstances in which graduated optimization can reach a global optimum, while keeping that result distinct from a claim about arbitrary nonconvex objectives.
icml-2016-on-graduated-optimization-for-.tldr: A graduated optimization algorithm has global convergence guarantees for a specified nonconvex function family, including under noisy gradient feedback.

paragraphs: Learning against other agents is difficult when those agents pursue competing goals and adapt their strategies. Their changing behavior makes the learning environment nonstationary, while interactions between strategies complicate prediction. This paper proposes neural models that jointly learn an agent’s policy and information about opponent behavior, bringing opponent modeling into deep reinforcement learning.

The approach encodes observations of opponents into a deep Q-network, rather than relying solely on explicit prediction of an opponent’s next action. It also retains explicit modeling within a multitasking setup. A mixture-of-experts architecture allows the model to discover different opponent strategy patterns without extra supervision, giving the representation a way to distinguish among different kinds of behavior.

The authors evaluate their models in a simulated soccer game and a popular trivia game. They report better performance than a deep Q-network and its variants. These results support incorporating opponent observations and strategy patterns into policy learning in the tested settings. The architectural contribution is to learn those representations alongside the agent’s own decision-making behavior.
icml-2016-opponent-modeling-in-deep-rein.tldr: Neural opponent models learn strategy patterns alongside a policy and outperform DQN variants in evaluated soccer and trivia games.

paragraphs: The paper tackles the problem of learning a probability distribution over natural images. An image model must capture complex visual relationships while remaining computationally manageable. The authors propose a deep neural network that predicts pixels sequentially across the two spatial dimensions, assigning discrete probabilities directly to raw pixel values.

This sequential construction encodes the full set of dependencies in an image. The architecture introduces fast two-dimensional recurrent layers and makes effective use of residual connections in deep recurrent networks. These components support a model that handles spatial relationships through successive predictions, with both the representation of image structure and the practicality of computation central to the design.

The authors report substantially improved log-likelihood scores over the previous state of the art on natural images. Their main results also establish benchmarks on the diverse ImageNet dataset. Generated samples are described as crisp, varied, and coherent at the whole-image level. The quantitative likelihood results and qualitative samples offer complementary evidence that the model captures meaningful structure in natural images.
icml-2016-pixel-recurrent-neural-network.tldr: A deep recurrent network models images through sequential pixel probabilities, improving reported likelihood scores and generating visually coherent samples.

paragraphs: Recommender systems are often trained and evaluated using data shaped by selection. Users choose what to interact with, and the recommendation system influences which items they encounter. Consequently, the available observations reflect those selection processes as well as user preferences. This paper treats that bias as a central issue in both learning recommendations and measuring their performance.

The authors adapt models and estimation techniques from causal inference to address the problem. Their approach produces unbiased performance estimators despite biased observations and leads to a matrix factorization method for prediction. Handling evaluation and training within the same approach matters because selection affects both the evidence used to compare systems and the data used to fit them.

On real-world data, the proposed matrix factorization method substantially improves prediction performance. The authors also examine robustness theoretically and empirically and find the approach practical and scalable. The contribution combines a principled way to correct recommendation evaluation with a learning method whose reported predictive improvements demonstrate the practical relevance of addressing selection bias.
icml-2016-recommendations-as-treatments-.tldr: Causal inference techniques address selection bias in recommendation data, enabling unbiased evaluation and improved matrix factorization predictions.

paragraphs: Stochastic Dual Newton Ascent, or SDNA, is an algorithm for minimizing regularized empirical loss. It works through the dual formulation of the learning problem and updates a randomly chosen subset of dual variables at each iteration. Its distinguishing feature is the ability to use all local curvature information contained in the examples.

Curvature describes how the optimization objective changes as the variables move, providing information beyond a gradient direction alone. The authors contrast SDNA with methods such as stochastic dual coordinate ascent and report substantial theoretical and practical improvements, sometimes by orders of magnitude. The benefit comes from making richer use of local structure within the randomly selected update.

The abstract gives a concrete description for an L2-regularized primal problem. In this case, the dual consists of a concave quadratic function plus a separable term. Each SDNA step solves a proximal subproblem involving a random principal submatrix of the quadratic function’s Hessian. This construction explains the Newton aspect of the method and how curvature enters its stochastic updates.
icml-2016-sdna-stochastic-dual-newton-as.tldr: SDNA uses local curvature in random dual-variable updates, delivering substantial theoretical and practical gains in some regularized learning problems.

paragraphs: This paper studies optimization methods for zero-sum, two-player Markov games through the Optimal Bellman Residual. That residual provides an objective for assessing agreement with the game’s optimality equations. The authors investigate how Newton and quasi-Newton methods relate to algorithms that improve policies by reducing this residual or a projected version of it.

They show that applying Newton’s method to a norm of the Optimal Bellman Residual produces Bellman Residual Minimization Policy Iteration. Applying it to a norm of the projected residual produces Least Squares Policy Iteration. These relationships provide a common optimization interpretation of the two algorithms and motivate replacing their Newton-based updates with quasi-Newton alternatives.

The proposed algorithms require only modest coding changes to the existing methods. The authors report significant improvements in stability and performance at low cost, illustrated through an experiment on artificially constructed games called Garnets. The contribution combines an explanation of familiar policy-iteration methods with practical modifications whose benefits are demonstrated in that experimental setting.
icml-2016-softened-approximate-policy-it.tldr: A Newton-method interpretation of policy iteration motivates quasi-Newton variants that improve stability and performance in experiments on artificial Markov games.

paragraphs: This paper develops a limited-memory stochastic block BFGS update for optimization methods that use sampled information. The goal is to incorporate richer curvature information into those methods. Curvature captures how the objective bends as parameters change, and the algorithm maintains an estimate of the inverse Hessian to use that information when forming updates.

At each iteration, the inverse-Hessian estimate is updated from a random sketch of the Hessian: a compressed representation of its curvature information. The authors propose several ways to construct these sketches. They then build a quasi-Newton method that combines the block BFGS updates with SVRG, a variance-reduction approach used to compute batch stochastic gradients.

The paper proves linear convergence for the resulting method, providing a theoretical result alongside the algorithmic construction. Numerical experiments on large-scale logistic regression problems show greater robustness and substantial improvements over the state-of-the-art methods used for comparison. These findings support combining compressed curvature information with variance-reduced gradients in the evaluated optimization problems.
icml-2016-stochastic-block-bfgs-squeezin.tldr: Random Hessian sketches enrich stochastic block BFGS updates, yielding a variance-reduced method with linear convergence and strong logistic regression results.

paragraphs: Partial Least Squares models covariance relationships between two data matrices. This paper considers its use in representation learning when multiple views of the data are available during training. The objective is to learn representations that capture relationships across those views, making PLS relevant to how the different data descriptions vary together.

The authors argue for treating PLS as a stochastic optimization problem with a population objective estimated from samples. This changes the emphasis from solving only for a particular fixed dataset to using observed data to optimize a broader statistical target. They identify this perspective as especially useful in large-data settings, where stochastic approximation methods are a natural computational choice.

The paper develops stochastic approximation algorithms for PLS, including approaches motivated by stochastic gradient descent, and provides bounds on their iteration complexity. Those bounds give a rigorous way to analyze the proposed methods’ computational requirements. The main contribution is thus both a formulation of multiview PLS and an analysis of algorithms suited to learning from sampled data.
icml-2016-stochastic-optimization-for-mu.tldr: Recasting multiview Partial Least Squares as population-level stochastic optimization enables sampling-based algorithms with iteration complexity guarantees.

paragraphs: The paper proposes a Bayesian neural network whose parameter uncertainty is represented using distributions over matrices. Specifically, a matrix-variate Gaussian posterior models covariance across each layer’s input and output dimensions. This structure allows the model to represent relationships among parameters, making correlations an explicit part of the uncertainty description.

Using approximate covariance matrices, the authors obtain a representation of those correlations that can be cheaper than fully factorized parameter posteriors. They also show that applying local reparameterization gives the hidden units in each layer a Gaussian process interpretation. This establishes a connection between the proposed neural network and deep Gaussian processes, linking two ways of describing probabilistic models.

The authors use that connection to introduce pseudo-data into the model, enabling more efficient posterior sampling while preserving the original model’s properties. Extensive experiments are reported as validating the approach. The contribution combines structured parameter uncertainty, economical covariance representation, and an alternative interpretation that leads directly to a further improvement in sampling efficiency.
icml-2016-structured-and-efficient-varia.tldr: Matrix-Gaussian parameter posteriors capture neural-network correlations efficiently and connect to Gaussian processes to enable improved posterior sampling.

paragraphs: The paper studies variable selection in linear regression when features come in groups. The goal is to identify groups with a nonzero effect on the response while controlling false discoveries. This makes a group, rather than an individual feature, the unit at which a selected result is judged relevant or irrelevant.

The authors propose the group knockoff filter for this setting. By defining discoveries at the group level and using the grouping structure, the method gains power relative to sparse regression methods. They also apply it to multitask regression, where several response variables share similar patterns of relevant features. In that setting, shared sparsity provides structure that the selection procedure can use.

Empirically, the method controls false discoveries at the group level in both grouped-feature and multitask regression. It also makes substantially more discoveries by exploiting the available group structure. These findings indicate that organizing selection around meaningful groups can improve the ability to find relevant effects while maintaining the stated group-level error control.
icml-2016-the-knockoff-filter-for-fdr-co.tldr: The group knockoff filter uses grouped structure to find more relevant feature groups while empirically controlling group-level false discoveries.

paragraphs: Structured prediction produces outputs with internal organization, such as image segmentations or parse trees. Finding the highest-scoring output can be formulated as an integer linear program. Rich scoring functions make this computation difficult, so both training and prediction often depend on approximate solvers. A common approach replaces the integer problem with a linear programming relaxation.

The paper asks why these relaxations are often tight on real-world instances. Tightness means that the relaxed optimization retains a solution consistent with the original discrete problem. This is valuable because the computational relaxation can then recover the desired discrete solution. The authors propose a theoretical explanation centered on the interaction between learning and approximate inference.

They show that training with LP-relaxed inference encourages integral solutions on training examples and that tightness generalizes from training to test data. This connects observed inference behavior to the learning procedure itself. The result explains why tightness can persist on unseen examples, without turning the empirical observation that relaxations are often tight into a claim that they always are.
icml-2016-train-and-test-tightness-of-lp.tldr: Training with LP-relaxed inference encourages integral solutions, and the paper shows how this tightness can generalize to test examples.

paragraphs: The paper examines the individual decision problems that arise during Tetris and finds that most are easy in a particular sense. A player or learning algorithm can often choose well among the available moves without already knowing an evaluation function that performs well over the whole game. Local choices can therefore be simpler than learning an effective overall scoring rule.

The authors attribute this to three conditions that occur frequently in the game: simple dominance, cumulative dominance, and noncompensation. These conditions provide structure for comparing actions, reducing dependence on a fully learned evaluation function. Their importance is that the available moves themselves can contain enough structure to support a good choice before the complete scoring problem has been solved.

The paper argues that exploiting these properties can produce faster and more effective learning algorithms and make certain forms of domain knowledge easy to incorporate. The authors also suggest that Tetris is unlikely to be unusual among sequential decision problems in possessing these properties. That broader relevance is proposed as a possibility rather than demonstrated for all such problems.
icml-2016-why-most-decisions-are-easy-in.tldr: Many Tetris choices can be made well without a strong overall evaluation function because recurring structural conditions simplify action comparisons.
